You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The structure is described in the monoclinic space group Cm (number 8, Hall symbol C -2y), using a nonstandard input cell rather than the conventional symmetry cell. The supplied input lattice has parameters a = 5.72850484 Å, b = 5.72850484 Å, c = 10.74853232 Å, with interaxial angles α = 89.6866166°, β = 89.6866166°, and γ = 41.87573831°. The declared input composition is Zr₆N₄O₆, corresponding to 16 atoms in the input cell. All atomic positions are given as fractional coordinates, and the relation between the input and standard frames is q_standard = P q_input + s, with s = (0, 0, 0). The transformation matrix P has rows (−1/2, −1/2, 0), (1/2, −1/2, 0), and (1.1580057090914883 × 10⁻¹⁹, 1.1580057090914883 × 10⁻¹⁹, 1), so the standard-frame coordinates are obtained essentially by x_std = −(x_in + y_in)/2, y_std = (x_in − y_in)/2, and z_std = z_in, apart from the numerically negligible 10⁻¹⁹ terms in the last row. Coordinate values are reported to six decimal places, and no positional corrections beyond this rounding are required.

In the standard description, every independent atom lies on the mirror plane y = 0 and belongs to a doubly degenerate 2a orbit of the form (x, 0, z), with the C-centered monoclinic symmetry generating the second member of each pair. There are six crystallographically independent zirconium orbits. The first Zr orbit is at (0.144597, 0, 0.565641); the second at (0.146000, 0, 0.937105); the third at (0.193332, 0, 0.248210); the fourth at (0.806966, 0, 0.756329); the fifth at (0.858374, 0, 0.058813); and the sixth at (0.862531, 0, 0.437403). These six independent Zr positions, each of multiplicity two, account for the six zirconium atoms in the input composition.

The nitrogen sublattice is described by four independent 2a orbits, also confined to y = 0. Their representative positions are (0.298752, 0, 0.426536), (0.301924, 0, 0.080577), (0.235849, 0, 0.744762), and (0.701842, 0, 0.925613). Together these four multiplicity-two nitrogen orbits give the four nitrogen atoms of the input cell.

Oxygen occupies six further independent 2a orbits on the same mirror plane. The representative oxygen positions are (0.045434, 0, 0.117277), (0.043006, 0, 0.381421), (0.953721, 0, 0.612980), (0.955633, 0, 0.883939), (0.695011, 0, 0.571279), and (0.757026, 0, 0.252115). These six multiplicity-two oxygen orbits complete the six oxygen atoms required by the stated composition.

Thus, the full three-dimensional structure is generated by placing all sixteen independent representative atoms on the y = 0 mirror plane at the fractional coordinates above, applying the Cm symmetry operations to duplicate each orbit, and then transforming back to the original nonstandard input cell through the inverse of the stated relation q_standard = P q_input + s. The result is a C-centered monoclinic arrangement in which the zirconium, nitrogen, and oxygen sublattices are all built from independent (x, 0, z) pairs repeated by the space-group symmetry, with the input cell geometry and composition preserved exactly as supplied.
